09-information-constraints.question: For which of these input sets can one fixed unitary (with any environment) copy every member exactly? (a) \(\{\ket0,\ket1\}\); (b) \(\{\ket+,\ket-\}\); (c) \(\{\ket0,\ket+\}\); (d) \(\{\ket0,-\ket0\}\). Use the condition \(s\le s^2\) on the overlap magnitude.
hints: The overlap condition allows only \(s=0\) or \(s=1\).
\(\ket0\) and \(-\ket0\) are the same physical state.
09-information-constraints.answer: (a) and (b) are orthogonal pairs, \(s=0\), so copying is allowed; a CNOT copies (a), and \(H\) followed by CNOT and \(H\otimes H\) copies (b). (c) has \(s=1/\sqrt2\), and \(s\le s^2\) fails: no cloner exists. (d) has \(s=1\): the two vectors describe one physical state, and re-preparing it is trivially possible. Only sets of mutually orthogonal (or identical) states can be cloned deterministically.

09-information-constraints.question: Can one channel broadcast both members of each family? (a) \(\mathrm{diag}(0.7,0.3)\) and \(\mathrm{diag}(0.2,0.8)\); (b) \(\mathrm{diag}(0.7,0.3)\) and \(\ket+\bra+\). Decide by checking whether the matrices commute.
hints: Diagonal matrices always commute.
Compute \(\rho\sigma\) and \(\sigma\rho\) for (b).
09-information-constraints.answer: (a) Both are diagonal, so they commute and can be broadcast: measure \(Z\) and write the result into two registers. (b) \(\mathrm{diag}(0.7,0.3)\,\ket+\bra+=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}0.7&0.7\\0.3&0.3\end{pmatrix}\), while the reverse product is \(\frac12\begin{pmatrix}0.7&0.3\\0.7&0.3\end{pmatrix}\). They differ, so the pair does not commute and, by the broadcasting theorem, no channel gives both outputs the correct marginals for both inputs.

09-information-constraints.question: Alice and Bob share \(\ket{\Phi^+}\). Alice resets her qubit to \(\ket0\) (swap with a fresh ancilla and discard). Find the new joint state and Bob’s reduced state. Has Alice’s drastic operation signalled anything to Bob?
hints: Discarding Alice’s original qubit leaves Bob with its partner’s reduced state.
The new joint state is a product.
09-information-constraints.answer: After the reset, Alice holds \(\ket0\), unentangled with Bob, and Bob’s qubit is the reduced state of the original pair: \(\rho_B=I/2\). The joint state is \(\ket0\bra0\otimes I/2\). Bob’s statistics are exactly what they were before, even though Alice destroyed the entanglement. Any trace-preserving local operation leaves the other party’s reduced state unchanged, which is the content of no-signalling.

09-information-constraints.question: CNOT copies basis states. Use it as an attempted cloner on \(\ket\psi=\cos\theta\ket0+\sin\theta\ket1\) with a blank target. (a) Find the overlap of the output with the ideal two copies \(\ket\psi\ket\psi\), and the fidelity (its squared magnitude). (b) Find the fidelity of one output qubit’s reduced state with \(\ket\psi\). (c) Evaluate both at \(\theta=0\) and \(\theta=\pi/4\).
hints: The output is \(\cos\theta\ket{00}+\sin\theta\ket{11}\).
Each output qubit has reduced state \(\mathrm{diag}(\cos^2\theta,\sin^2\theta)\).
09-information-constraints.answer: (a) \(\braket{\psi\psi}{\text{out}}=\cos\theta\cos^2\theta+\sin\theta\sin^2\theta=\cos^3\theta+\sin^3\theta\), so the fidelity is \((\cos^3\theta+\sin^3\theta)^2\). (b) Each output is \(\mathrm{diag}(\cos^2\theta,\sin^2\theta)\), with fidelity \(\bra\psi\rho\ket\psi=\cos^4\theta+\sin^4\theta\). (c) At \(\theta=0\) both are \(1\): basis states are copied perfectly. At \(\theta=\pi/4\) (\(\ket+\)) the joint fidelity is \(\big(2\cdot2^{-3/2}\big)^2=\frac12\) and each output has fidelity \(\frac12\): the outputs are maximally mixed rather than copies. A copier designed for one basis does poorly on superpositions.

09-information-constraints.question: Alice and Bob share \(\ket\Psi=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}(\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{11})\). Alice measures in the \(\pm\) basis and does not report the result. (a) Find the probability of each of her outcomes and Bob’s conditional state. (b) Compute Bob’s probability of \(0\) averaged over her outcomes, and compare with his probability before her measurement.
hints: \((\bra+\otimes I)\ket\Psi=\frac{1}{\sqrt6}(\ket0+2\ket1)\).
\((\bra-\otimes I)\ket\Psi=\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\ket0\).
09-information-constraints.answer: (a) Outcome \(+\) has probability \(\frac16(1+4)=\frac56\) and leaves Bob in \((\ket0+2\ket1)/\sqrt5\); outcome \(-\) has probability \(\frac16\) and leaves Bob in \(\ket0\). (b) Bob’s probability of \(0\) is \(\frac56\cdot\frac15+\frac16\cdot1=\frac13\). Before Alice measured, it was \(|\alpha_{00}|^2+|\alpha_{10}|^2=\frac13\). The conditional states are very different, but the average is the same, as the completeness argument of Section 9.2.1 guarantees for every local operation.

09-information-constraints.question: Show that perfect cloning would allow signalling. Alice and Bob share many Bell pairs; for each pair, Alice measures either all in \(Z\) or all in \(X\), to send one bit. Suppose Bob could make \(10\) copies of his qubit. What would he observe on the copies in each case, and how could he read Alice’s choice? What does this say about the relation between no-cloning and no-signalling?
hints: If Alice measured \(Z\), Bob’s qubit is \(\ket0\) or \(\ket1\); if \(X\), it is \(\ket+\) or \(\ket-\).
Measure all copies in \(Z\) and see whether they agree.
09-information-constraints.answer: If Alice measured \(Z\), Bob’s qubit is \(\ket0\) or \(\ket1\), and ten copies measured in \(Z\) all give the same result. If she measured \(X\), his qubit is \(\ket+\) or \(\ket-\), and ten \(Z\) measurements give independent fair bits, all agreeing with probability only \(2\cdot2^{-10}\approx0.002\). So Bob could read Alice’s choice, and hence a message, instantly, with an error under \(1\%\). Since no-signalling holds for every local operation, a perfect cloner cannot exist. No-cloning is part of what keeps quantum correlations from carrying messages without communication.

09-information-constraints.question: For the commuting family \(\rho_q=q\ket0\bra0+(1-q)\ket1\bra1\), the broadcaster measures \(Z\) and writes the result into two registers. For \(q=0.8\), compute the probability that the two outputs agree, and compare with two independent samples from \(\rho_q\otimes\rho_q\). Find the mutual information between the two outputs in each case.
hints: The broadcast outputs always agree.
Independent samples agree with probability \(q^2+(1-q)^2\).
09-information-constraints.answer: The broadcast output \(0.8\ket{00}\bra{00}+0.2\ket{11}\bra{11}\) gives agreeing bits with probability \(1\), while independent samples agree with probability \(0.64+0.04=0.68\). The broadcast outputs share \(h_2(0.2)\approx0.722\) bits of mutual information (each output determines the other), while independent copies share none. Both have the correct marginal \(\rho_q\). Broadcasting reproduces each part correctly but correlates the parts, which is why it is weaker than copying.

09-information-constraints.question: A student argues: “No-cloning says a quantum state cannot exist in two places, so teleportation, which makes Bob’s qubit equal to Alice’s input, must violate it.” Explain why it does not, describing what happens to Alice’s system during the protocol.
hints: After Alice’s measurement, what state does her input qubit hold?
Is there ever a moment when two systems both hold the unknown state?
09-information-constraints.answer: In teleportation Alice measures her input qubit together with her half of the Bell pair. After the measurement, her qubits are in definite basis states that carry no information about the input amplitudes. Bob’s qubit becomes the input state only after he applies the correction selected by her classical message. At no time do two systems both hold the unknown state, so nothing is copied: the state is transferred, and the original is consumed. No-cloning forbids duplication, not relocation.

09-information-constraints.question: A measure-and-prepare cloner measures \(Z\) and prepares two copies of the outcome state. (a) Find the fidelity of each copy with the input for \(\ket0\), \(\ket1\), \(\ket\pm\), and \((\ket0\pm i\ket1)/\sqrt2\). (b) Average over these six inputs. (c) Compare with the known optimal universal cloner, whose copies have fidelity \(\frac56\) for every input.
hints: For \(\ket+\), each copy is \(\ket0\) or \(\ket1\) with probability \(\frac12\).
Fidelity of \(\ket j\) with \(\ket\psi\) is \(|\braket j\psi|^2\).
09-information-constraints.answer: (a) For \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\) the copies are perfect: fidelity \(1\). For the other four inputs, the copies are \(\ket0\) or \(\ket1\) at random, each with fidelity \(\frac12\) with the input. (b) The average is \(\frac16(1+1+4\cdot\frac12)=\frac23\). (c) The optimal universal cloner of Bužek and Hillery reaches \(\frac56\) for every input, without favoring a basis. Approximate cloning is possible, but with fidelity strictly below \(1\); better cloners must keep the copies entangled rather than measuring first.

09-information-constraints.question: Construct a probabilistic exact cloner for \(\{\ket0,\ket+\}\) from unambiguous discrimination: on a conclusive outcome, prepare two copies of the identified state; otherwise declare failure. (a) What is its success probability? (b) Why does it not violate no-cloning? (c) The optimal probabilistic cloner for two states with overlap \(s\) succeeds with probability \(1/(1+s)\). Evaluate it and compare.
hints: Unambiguous discrimination succeeds with probability \(1-s\).
No-cloning forbids deterministic exact copying.
09-information-constraints.answer: (a) With \(s=1/\sqrt2\), unambiguous discrimination succeeds with probability \(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx0.293\), and on success Bob knows the state and prepares as many copies as he likes. (b) The procedure sometimes fails and says so; no-cloning forbids only an exact copier that always succeeds on every member of a nonorthogonal set. (c) \(1/(1+s)\approx0.586\), the Duan–Guo bound, which is achieved by a cloner that does not first identify the state. Asking for exactly two copies, rather than full knowledge, roughly doubles the success probability.

10-entanglement-protocols.question: Teleport \(\ket\psi=\ket1\). For Alice’s outcomes \(01\) and \(11\), write Bob’s state before correction and check that his corrections recover \(\ket1\).
hints: Bob holds \(X^nZ^m\ket\psi\) and applies \(X^n\), then \(Z^m\).
10-entanglement-protocols.answer: For \(01\) (\(m=0,n=1\)), Bob holds \(X\ket1=\ket0\) and applies \(X\), recovering \(\ket1\). For \(11\), he holds \(XZ\ket1=X(-\ket1)=-\ket0\); applying \(X\) gives \(-\ket1\), then \(Z\) gives \(\ket1\). The input was a basis state, yet Bob still needs both bits: without them he cannot tell \(\ket0\) from \(\ket1\) in his hands, and his unconditioned state is \(I/2\).

10-entanglement-protocols.question: In dense coding, trace the decoder (CNOT from Alice’s received qubit to Bob’s, then \(H\) on the received qubit) for the messages \(01\) and \(11\), starting from the encoded states in the table.
hints: CNOT maps \(\ket{\Psi^\pm}\) to \(\ket\pm\ket1\).
\(H\ket\pm\) gives \(\ket0\) or \(\ket1\).
10-entanglement-protocols.answer: Message \(01\): the encoded state is \((\ket{01}+\ket{10})/\sqrt2\); CNOT gives \((\ket{01}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2=\ket+\ket1\), and \(H\) gives \(\ket{01}\). Message \(11\): the encoded state is \((\ket{10}-\ket{01})/\sqrt2\); CNOT gives \((\ket{11}-\ket{01})/\sqrt2=-\ket-\ket1\), and \(H\) gives \(-\ket{11}\). Both decode correctly with certainty; the sign is global.

10-entanglement-protocols.question: Count the resources: (a) teleporting five unknown qubits; (b) sending ten classical bits by dense coding; (c) sending ten classical bits with no shared entanglement, one bit per transmitted qubit. Which resources does each consume?
hints: Teleportation: one ebit and two bits per qubit.
Dense coding: one ebit and one transmitted qubit per two bits.
10-entanglement-protocols.answer: (a) Five shared Bell pairs and ten classical bits; no qubit is sent during the protocol. (b) Five Bell pairs and five transmitted qubits. (c) Ten transmitted qubits (or ten classical bits sent directly). Dense coding halves the qubits sent only by spending pre-shared entanglement, which itself required sending qubits earlier. Protocol comparisons must count every resource, including entanglement distributed in advance.

10-entanglement-protocols.question: In dense coding, Alice’s qubit suffers a phase flip \(Z\) with probability \(p\) on its way to Bob. (a) Show that a \(Z\) on Alice’s qubit after encoding \(X^bZ^a\) turns the encoded state into the one for message \((a\oplus1,b)\), up to sign. (b) Find the probability that each decoded bit is wrong. (c) What happens with bit-flip noise \(X\) instead?
hints: \(ZX^bZ^a=\pm X^bZ^{a+1}\).
An \(X\) error changes \(b\).
10-entanglement-protocols.answer: (a) \(ZX^bZ^a=(-1)^bX^bZ^{a\oplus1}\), so the joint state becomes, up to sign, the encoding of \((a\oplus1,b)\). (b) The decoder then returns \(a\oplus1\): the first bit is wrong with probability \(p\), and the second bit is always right. (c) An \(X\) error gives \(X^{b\oplus1}Z^a\), so the second bit is wrong with probability \(p\) and the first is untouched. Each Pauli error on the transmitted qubit maps one Bell state to another, so the noise appears as a classical error on specific message bits.

10-entanglement-protocols.question: Teleportation is attempted with the shared pair \(\ket{\Phi^-}=(\ket{00}-\ket{11})/\sqrt2\) by mistake, and Bob applies the usual corrections. (a) Using \(\ket{\Phi^-}=(I\otimes Z)\ket{\Phi^+}\), show that Bob ends with \(Z\ket\psi\) up to sign in every branch. (b) For which inputs is the protocol still correct? (c) How could the error be repaired?
hints: A \(Z\) on Bob’s qubit commutes with all of Alice’s operations.
\(Z^mX^nZX^nZ^m=(-1)^nZ\).
10-entanglement-protocols.answer: (a) The \(Z\) acts on Bob’s qubit, which Alice never touches, so in each branch Bob holds \(ZX^nZ^m\ket\psi\). His correction gives \(Z^mX^nZX^nZ^m\ket\psi=(-1)^nZ\ket\psi\), using \(XZX=-Z\) and \(Z^mZZ^m=Z\). (b) The output equals the input (up to phase) only for eigenstates of \(Z\), \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\); for \(\ket+\) Bob receives \(\ket-\), an orthogonal state. (c) If the pair is known to be \(\ket{\Phi^-}\), Bob adds a final \(Z\). Teleportation transfers whatever Pauli error the shared pair carries onto the output, so the quality of the shared entanglement sets the quality of the transfer.

10-entanglement-protocols.question: In entanglement swapping with order \(A,B,C,D\), the initial state is \(\frac12(\ket{0000}+\ket{0011}+\ket{1100}+\ket{1111})\). Project \(B,C\) onto \(\ket{\Psi^-}=(\ket{01}-\ket{10})/\sqrt2\), find the probability of this outcome, and identify the endpoints’ state.
hints: Only terms with \(BC=01\) or \(BC=10\) survive.
10-entanglement-protocols.answer: Only \(\ket{0011}\) (\(BC=01\), \(AD=01\)) and \(\ket{1100}\) (\(BC=10\), \(AD=10\)) survive. The projection gives \(\frac12\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{01}_{AD}-\ket{10}_{AD})\), with squared length \(\frac14\), so the outcome has probability \(\frac14\) and leaves the endpoints in \(\ket{\Psi^-}\). The middle measurement outcome names which Bell state \(A\) and \(D\) now share; without that record, the four equally likely possibilities average to \(I/4\).

10-entanglement-protocols.question: Show that the classical record \((m,n)\) sent in teleportation carries no information about \(\ket\psi\). (a) Find the joint probability of \((m,n)\) for any input. (b) Suppose Eve copies the two bits but has no access to Bob’s qubit. What does she learn? (c) What could Eve do with Bob’s qubit alone, without the bits?
hints: Every branch has squared length \(\frac14\) regardless of \(\alpha,\beta\).
Bob’s unconditioned state is \(I/2\).
10-entanglement-protocols.answer: (a) Each of the four outcomes has probability \(\frac14\) for every input, so the record is uniformly random and independent of \(\ket\psi\). (b) Eve learns nothing about \(\alpha,\beta\): the bits are statistically identical for every input. (c) Without the bits, Bob’s qubit (or Eve’s, if she stole it) is in \(I/2\) for every input, again carrying no information. The input’s description resides in the correlation between the bits and the qubit; neither part alone reveals it.

10-entanglement-protocols.question: A student says: “Bob must apply \(X^n\) before \(Z^m\); in the other order, outcome \(11\) leaves him with the wrong state.” Check what happens if Bob applies \(Z\) first and then \(X\) in branch \(11\), where he holds \(XZ\ket\psi\).
hints: Compute \(XZ\cdot XZ\).
10-entanglement-protocols.answer: Applying \(Z\), then \(X\), gives \(XZ\,XZ\ket\psi\). Since \(ZX=-XZ\), \(XZXZ=-XXZZ=-I\), so Bob holds \(-\ket\psi\). That differs from \(\ket\psi\) only by a global phase, which no measurement detects. The order of the two corrections does not matter for teleporting a standalone qubit. It would matter if Bob’s qubit were later used as the control of an operation, or if the correction were itself controlled, because the sign would then become a relative phase between branches.

10-entanglement-protocols.question: Alice’s input qubit \(S\) is half of an entangled pair with a reference \(R\): \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{0}_R\ket{0}_S+\ket1_R\ket1_S)\). She teleports \(S\) to Bob. (a) Use linearity of the branch formula to show that, after Bob’s correction, \(R\) and \(B\) share the same entangled state. (b) What does this say about teleportation as a channel? (c) Relate the result to entanglement swapping.
hints: Apply the branch formula separately to the \(\ket0_S\) and \(\ket1_S\) terms.
The correction \(Z^mX^n\) does not depend on the input.
10-entanglement-protocols.answer: (a) The branch formula holds for each basis input, and Alice’s operations and Bob’s correction do not depend on the input, so by linearity the whole superposition is carried through: in every branch, after correction, the state is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0_R\ket0_B+\ket1_R\ket1_B)\). (b) Teleportation acts as the identity channel on \(S\), including on correlations with systems it never touches; it transfers states, entanglement included, not just a list of amplitudes. (c) This is entanglement swapping: teleporting one half of a Bell pair entangles the other half with the receiver, which is how quantum repeaters extend entanglement across links.

10-entanglement-protocols.question: Dense coding sends two classical bits with one transmitted qubit and one ebit. Could a cleverer encoding send three bits with the same resources? Use the facts that Bob ends up holding two qubits, a four-dimensional system, and that at most \(\log_2d\) bits can be reliably read from a \(d\)-dimensional system (the Holevo bound). Also explain why, without the shared pair, one transmitted qubit carries at most one bit.
hints: Count the dimension of everything Bob can measure.
Without entanglement, Bob receives only the one qubit.
10-entanglement-protocols.answer: After the transmission Bob holds two qubits, and every message must be decoded by a measurement on that four-dimensional system. At most \(\log_24=2\) bits can be reliably extracted, so dense coding is optimal: three bits are impossible. Without prior entanglement, Bob receives only one qubit, of dimension \(2\), giving at most \(\log_22=1\) bit. The shared pair doubles the capacity by letting Alice’s local operation choose among four orthogonal joint states, not by making one qubit hold more than its dimension allows.

11-quantum-entropy.question: Find the von Neumann entropy of \(\rho=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&r\\r&1\end{pmatrix}\) for \(r=0.6\), and compare it with the Shannon entropy of its computational-basis outcomes.
hints: The eigenvalues are \((1\pm r)/2\).
11-quantum-entropy.answer: The eigenvalues are \(0.8\) and \(0.2\), so \(S(\rho)=h_2(0.2)\approx0.722\) bits. A computational-basis measurement gives fair outcomes, with Shannon entropy \(1\) bit. The measurement record is more uncertain than the state, because the computational basis is not the eigenbasis; measuring in the \(\pm\) basis would give outcome entropy \(0.722\), matching \(S\).

11-quantum-entropy.question: For the pure state \(\cos\frac\pi8\ket{00}+\sin\frac\pi8\ket{11}\), find \(S(A)\), \(S(B)\), \(S(AB)\), \(I(A:B)\), and \(S(A\mid B)\).
hints: The reduced state of \(A\) is \(\mathrm{diag}(\cos^2\frac\pi8,\sin^2\frac\pi8)\approx\mathrm{diag}(0.854,0.146)\).
A pure joint state has \(S(AB)=0\).
11-quantum-entropy.answer: \(S(A)=S(B)=h_2(0.854)\approx0.601\) bits, and \(S(AB)=0\) because the joint state is pure. So \(I(A:B)\approx1.202\) bits and \(S(A\mid B)\approx-0.601\). This partially entangled state sits between a product (\(I=0\), \(S(A\mid B)=0\)) and a Bell pair (\(I=2\), \(S(A\mid B)=-1\)). For pure joint states, \(S(A)\) measures the entanglement.

11-quantum-entropy.question: Show that \(D(\rho\|I/2)=1-S(\rho)\) for any qubit state \(\rho\), and evaluate it for \(\ket0\bra0\), \(\mathrm{diag}(\frac34,\frac14)\), and \(I/2\).
hints: \(\mathrm{tr}(\rho\log_2\rho)=-S(\rho)\).
11-quantum-entropy.answer: Since \(\log_2(I/2)=-I\), \(D(\rho\|I/2)=\mathrm{tr}(\rho\log_2\rho)+\mathrm{tr}\rho=1-S(\rho)\). For \(\ket0\bra0\) it is \(1\); for \(\mathrm{diag}(\frac34,\frac14)\), \(1-0.811\approx0.189\); for \(I/2\), \(0\). Relative entropy to the maximally mixed state measures how far a state is from complete uncertainty, in bits.

11-quantum-entropy.question: Two pure states with overlap magnitude \(s\) are used with equal priors. (a) Show that the average state \(\bar\rho\) has eigenvalues \((1\pm s)/2\), so the Holevo quantity is \(\chi=h_2\big(\frac{1+s}{2}\big)\). (b) Evaluate for \(s=0\), \(s=1/\sqrt2\), and \(s=1\). (c) Check part (a) for \(\ket+\) and \(\ket{y_+}\).
hints: \(\bar\rho\) has trace \(1\) and determinant \(\frac14(1-s^2)\).
Use the decomposition \(\ket\phi=s\ket\psi+\sqrt{1-s^2}\ket{\psi_\perp}\) after fixing the phase.
11-quantum-entropy.answer: (a) In the basis \(\ket\psi,\ket{\psi_\perp}\), \(\bar\rho=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1+s^2&s\sqrt{1-s^2}\\s\sqrt{1-s^2}&1-s^2\end{pmatrix}\), with trace \(1\) and determinant \(\frac14(1-s^2)\). The eigenvalues solve \(\lambda^2-\lambda+\frac14(1-s^2)=0\), giving \((1\pm s)/2\). Pure components contribute no entropy, so \(\chi=h_2(\frac{1+s}{2})\). (b) \(s=0\): \(1\) bit; \(s=1/\sqrt2\): \(h_2(0.854)\approx0.601\); \(s=1\): \(0\). (c) \(\frac12(\ket+\bra++\ket{y_+}\bra{y_+})=\frac14\begin{pmatrix}2&1-i\\1+i&2\end{pmatrix}\) has eigenvalues \(\frac14(2\pm|1-i|)=\frac{2\pm\sqrt2}{4}\), as predicted with \(s=1/\sqrt2\).

11-quantum-entropy.question: A noisy Bell pair is \(\rho=(1-p)\ket{\Phi^+}\bra{\Phi^+}+pI/4\). (a) Find its eigenvalues. (b) Compute \(S(AB)\), \(I(A:B)\), and \(S(A\mid B)\) for \(p=0.2\) and \(p=0.5\). (c) Interpret the sign of the conditional entropy.
hints: \(\ket{\Phi^+}\) has eigenvalue \(1-p+\frac p4\); the three orthogonal Bell states each have \(\frac p4\).
Each marginal is \(I/2\).
11-quantum-entropy.answer: (a) \(1-\frac{3p}{4}\) once and \(\frac p4\) three times. (b) Each marginal is \(I/2\), so \(S(A)=S(B)=1\). For \(p=0.2\): eigenvalues \(0.85,0.05,0.05,0.05\), \(S(AB)\approx0.848\), \(I\approx1.152\), \(S(A\mid B)\approx-0.152\). For \(p=0.5\): eigenvalues \(0.625\) and three of \(0.125\), \(S(AB)\approx1.549\), \(I\approx0.451\), \(S(A\mid B)\approx+0.549\). (c) At \(p=0.2\) the conditional entropy is still negative, a signature of entanglement usable in state merging; at \(p=0.5\) it is positive. Noise raises the joint entropy above the marginal entropy and removes this quantum advantage (although a state with positive \(S(A\mid B)\) can still be entangled).

11-quantum-entropy.question: For the pure state \(\frac{1}{\sqrt3}(\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{11})\), find both reduced density matrices, show that they have the same eigenvalues, and compute \(S(A)=S(B)\).
hints: \(\rho_A=\begin{pmatrix}2/3&1/3\\1/3&1/3\end{pmatrix}\); compute \(\rho_B\) the same way, pairing equal Alice labels.
Both have trace \(1\) and determinant \(\frac19\).
11-quantum-entropy.answer: \(\rho_A=\begin{pmatrix}\frac23&\frac13\\\frac13&\frac13\end{pmatrix}\) (the partial trace). For Bob, \((\rho_B)_{00}=|\alpha_{00}|^2+|\alpha_{10}|^2=\frac13\), \((\rho_B)_{11}=\frac23\), and \((\rho_B)_{01}=\alpha_{00}\alpha_{01}^*+\alpha_{10}\alpha_{11}^*=\frac13\). Both have trace \(1\) and determinant \(\frac29-\frac19=\frac19\), so both have eigenvalues \(\frac12\big(1\pm\sqrt{5}/3\big)\approx0.873,0.127\), and \(S(A)=S(B)\approx0.550\) bits. For every pure joint state the two parts have equal entropy, even when their matrices look different.

11-quantum-entropy.question: Compute \(D(\ket0\bra0\,\|\,\rho_p)\) and \(D(\rho_p\,\|\,\ket0\bra0)\) for \(\rho_p=\mathrm{diag}(1-p,p)\) with \(p=\frac14\). Interpret the asymmetry in terms of testing the hypothesis “the state is \(\rho_p\)” against “the state is \(\ket0\)”.
hints: The support of \(\rho_p\) includes \(\ket1\), which \(\ket0\bra0\) excludes.
11-quantum-entropy.answer: \(D(\ket0\bra0\|\rho_p)=\mathrm{tr}[\ket0\bra0(\log_2\ket0\bra0-\log_2\rho_p)]=-\log_2\frac34\approx0.415\) bits. The reverse is infinite: \(\rho_p\) has weight on \(\ket1\), which \(\ket0\bra0\) never produces. Operationally, a single outcome \(1\) refutes “\(\ket0\)” with certainty, so that hypothesis can be rejected quickly when \(\rho_p\) is true; but when the true state is \(\ket0\), every outcome is consistent with \(\rho_p\), and only the slow accumulation of zeros, at about \(0.415\) bits per copy, separates them.

11-quantum-entropy.question: A student estimates the entropy of a state by measuring in the computational basis and computing the Shannon entropy of the outcomes. Show with \(\rho=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&\frac12\\\frac12&1\end{pmatrix}\) that this overestimates \(S(\rho)\), and state which measurement gives the right value.
hints: The eigenvalues are \(\frac34\) and \(\frac14\).
Mixing probabilities (as the diagonal does) can only increase Shannon entropy.
11-quantum-entropy.answer: The computational-basis outcomes are fair, giving \(1\) bit, but \(S(\rho)=h_2(\frac14)\approx0.811\) bits. The outcome entropy of a measurement in any orthonormal basis is at least \(S(\rho)\), with equality in the eigenbasis, here \(\{\ket+,\ket-\}\). Off-diagonal entries represent order that a mismatched measurement scrambles into apparent randomness. A pure state such as \(\ket+\) shows the extreme case: \(S=0\), yet its computational-basis record has \(1\) bit of entropy.

11-quantum-entropy.question: The three trine states \(\ket{\psi_k}\), used with equal priors, have average state \(I/2\), so \(\chi=1\) bit. Compute the mutual information for two measurements: (a) the trine POVM \(E_k=\frac23\ket{\psi_k}\bra{\psi_k}\); (b) the “anti-trine” POVM \(E_k=\frac23\ket{\psi_k^\perp}\bra{\psi_k^\perp}\), where \(\ket{\psi_k^\perp}\) is orthogonal to \(\ket{\psi_k}\). Compare both with \(\chi\).
hints: (a) \(p(j\mid j)=\frac23\), \(p(k\mid j)=\frac16\). (b) \(p(j\mid j)=0\), \(p(k\mid j)=\frac12\) for \(k\neq j\).
In both cases the outcomes are uniform, so \(H(Y)=\log_23\).
11-quantum-entropy.answer: Both POVMs give uniform outcomes, \(H(Y)=\log_23\approx1.585\). (a) \(H(Y\mid X)=H(\frac23,\frac16,\frac16)\approx1.252\), so \(I\approx0.333\) bits. (b) Each input gives two outcomes with probability \(\frac12\), so \(H(Y\mid X)=1\) and \(I=\log_23-1\approx0.585\) bits, the known optimum for this ensemble. Both fall short of \(\chi=1\). The best measurement for guessing (a) is not the best for information (b), and the Holevo quantity is an upper bound that a single-copy measurement need not reach.

11-quantum-entropy.question: Check data processing for \(\rho=\ket+\bra+\) and \(\sigma=I/2\) under the phase-flip channel with probability \(p\). (a) Compute \(D(\rho\|\sigma)\). (b) Show that after the channel, \(D=1-h_2(p)\). (c) Confirm that the value never exceeds the original and explain the cases \(p=\frac12\) and \(p=1\).
hints: \(\sigma\) is unchanged by the channel.
The output \(\rho'\) has eigenvalues \(1-p\) and \(p\).
11-quantum-entropy.answer: (a) \(D(\ket+\bra+\|I/2)=1-S(\ket+\bra+)=1\). (b) The channel leaves \(I/2\) unchanged and maps \(\ket+\bra+\) to \((1-p)\ket+\bra++p\ket-\bra-\), with eigenvalues \(1-p,p\); by the earlier identity, \(D=1-h_2(p)\). (c) \(h_2(p)\ge0\), so \(D\le1\), consistent with the data-processing inequality. At \(p=\frac12\) the output is \(I/2\) and \(D=0\): the states are identical. At \(p=1\) the output is the pure \(\ket-\), and \(D=1\) again, because a known flip loses no distinguishability.

12-quantum-compression.question: Give the Schumacher compression rate, in qubits per signal, for these memoryless sources: (a) always \(\ket0\); (b) \(\ket0\) or \(\ket1\) with probabilities \(0.9\) and \(0.1\); (c) \(\ket0\) or \(\ket+\) with equal probability.
hints: The rate is \(S(\rho)\) of the average state.
For (c), the Holevo calculation found eigenvalues \((1\pm1/\sqrt2)/2\).
12-quantum-compression.answer: (a) \(S=0\): nothing needs to be sent, since the receiver can prepare \(\ket0\) himself. (b) \(S=h_2(0.1)\approx0.469\) qubits per signal. (c) \(S=h_2(0.854)\approx0.601\) qubits per signal, even though the label choice carries \(1\) bit of classical entropy. Overlapping signals are cheaper to store as quantum states than their labels would be as classical bits.

12-quantum-compression.question: For the source \(\ket{\psi_\pm}=(\sqrt3\ket0\pm\ket1)/2\), compare the fidelity of three crude “compressors” that send nothing: (a) the decoder outputs \(I/2\); (b) the decoder outputs \(\ket0\); (c) the encoder measures \(Z\) and the decoder re-prepares the outcome (which sends one classical bit).
hints: \(F=\bra{\psi_\pm}\sigma\ket{\psi_\pm}\).
\(|\braket0{\psi_\pm}|^2=\frac34\).
12-quantum-compression.answer: (a) \(F=\frac12\). (b) \(F=|\braket0{\psi_\pm}|^2=\frac34\). (c) The text found \(F=\frac58\). Sending nothing and always outputting \(\ket0\) beats measuring and resending, because the measurement scrambles the coherence while \(\ket0\) is simply the closest single state to both signals. None of these approaches \(F=1\); faithful recovery needs a coherent encoder that keeps the signals’ superpositions.

12-quantum-compression.question: How many qubits are needed to store a subspace of dimension \(D=4\), \(D=5\), and \(D=2^{86.1}\)? For a source with \(S=0.811\), \(n=100\), and \(\delta=0.05\), what block size in qubits does the typical-space bound give, and what rate?
hints: \(m=\lceil\log_2D\rceil\).
12-quantum-compression.answer: \(D=4\) needs \(2\) qubits, \(D=5\) needs \(3\), and \(D=2^{86.1}\) needs \(87\). For the source, \(n(S+\delta)=86.1\), so \(87\) qubits suffice for the typical subspace: a rate of \(0.87\) qubits per signal, above \(S\) because of \(\delta\) and rounding. As \(n\) grows with \(\delta\) shrinking, the rate approaches \(0.811\).

12-quantum-compression.question: Apply the three-signal toy compressor to the product state \(\ket{\psi_+}^{\otimes3}\), where \(\ket{\psi_+}=(\sqrt3\ket0+\ket1)/2\). The encoder projects onto the span of \(000,001,010,100\); on success it keeps the projected state, and on failure the decoder outputs \(\ket{000}\). (a) Find the success probability \(p\). (b) Show that the fidelity is \(p^2+(1-p)\,|\braket{000}{\psi_+^{\otimes3}}|^2\) and evaluate it.
hints: The amplitudes are \((\sqrt3/2)^3\) on \(000\) and \(\frac38\) on each string with one \(1\).
On success the overlap with the target is \(\sqrt p\), giving contribution \(p\cdot p\).
12-quantum-compression.answer: (a) \(p=\frac{27}{64}+3\cdot\frac{9}{64}=\frac{54}{64}\approx0.844\). (b) On success the normalized state \(P\ket\Psi/\sqrt p\) has overlap \(\bra\Psi P\ket\Psi/\sqrt p=\sqrt p\) with the target, contributing \(p\cdot p=p^2\). On failure, the output \(\ket{000}\) contributes \((1-p)|\braket{000}\Psi|^2=(1-p)\frac{27}{64}\). The fidelity is \(0.712+0.066\approx0.778\), using \(2\) qubits for \(3\) signals. A coherent compressor beats crude strategies, but the toy block is too short to be nearly faithful.

12-quantum-compression.question: A source emits \(\ket0\) or \(\ket+\) with equal probability, and Alice knows each label. Compare two ways of sending \(n\) signals to Bob: (a) send the labels classically; (b) Schumacher-compress the quantum signals. Give the asymptotic rates. Then explain which method remains available if Alice receives the signals from a device that hides the labels.
hints: Classical labels have entropy \(1\) bit each.
\(S(\bar\rho)\approx0.601\).
12-quantum-compression.answer: (a) The labels are fair bits, so classical compression needs \(1\) bit per signal; Bob then prepares the states himself. (b) Quantum compression needs \(S\approx0.601\) qubits per signal, fewer resources, because the signals overlap and the average state is far from maximally mixed. If the labels are hidden, (a) is impossible: Alice cannot identify nonorthogonal states reliably, and any attempt disturbs them. Schumacher compression never needs to know which signal was sent, since it acts coherently on the typical subspace.

12-quantum-compression.question: A stronger test of a compressor uses a reference system. Let \(\ket\Phi=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\ket0_R\ket0+\frac12\ket1_R\ket1\), which purifies \(\rho=\mathrm{diag}(\frac34,\frac14)\). The “compressor” measures the signal in \(Z\) and resends the outcome. (a) Find the output joint state. (b) Compute the entanglement fidelity \(\bra\Phi\sigma_{RS}\ket\Phi\). (c) Compare with the ensemble fidelity \(\frac58\).
hints: Measuring \(Z\) on the signal removes the cross terms between \(\ket{00}\) and \(\ket{11}\).
The entanglement fidelity is \(\sum_j\lambda_j^2\).
12-quantum-compression.answer: (a) Dephasing gives \(\sigma_{RS}=\frac34\ket{00}\bra{00}+\frac14\ket{11}\bra{11}\). (b) \(\bra\Phi\sigma\ket\Phi=\frac34\cdot\frac34+\frac14\cdot\frac14=\frac58\). (c) It equals the ensemble fidelity found in Section 12.1.2. A procedure that measures the eigenbasis destroys the coherence between the system and anything entangled with it; faithful compression must preserve such correlations, which is the criterion Schumacher’s theorem uses.

12-quantum-compression.question: For \(n=2\) signals from the source with eigenvalues \(\frac34,\frac14\), compress into one qubit. (a) List the four eigenstring weights. (b) Which two-dimensional subspace keeps the most weight, and how much? (c) What rate is this, and how does the retained weight compare with the three-signal, two-qubit toy compressor?
hints: Keep the largest weights.
12-quantum-compression.answer: (a) \(\frac9{16},\frac3{16},\frac3{16},\frac1{16}\). (b) Keep \(00\) and one of \(01,10\): weight \(\frac{12}{16}=0.75\). (c) The rate is \(\frac12\) qubit per signal, below \(S\approx0.811\), and the retained weight is \(0.75\), lower than the \(0.844\) of the three-signal toy compressor at rate \(\frac23\). Short blocks force a crude choice between rate and fidelity; the asymptotic theorem says the trade-off disappears only above \(S\) and only as \(n\to\infty\).

12-quantum-compression.question: A student writes: “A compressor is faithful if the decoded average density matrix equals the source’s average \(\rho\).” Give a procedure for the \(\ket{\psi_\pm}\) source that passes this test perfectly yet has fidelity \(\frac58\), and say what the correct criterion requires.
hints: Measuring in the eigenbasis leaves the average matrix unchanged.
Fidelity is computed signal by signal, or with a reference.
12-quantum-compression.answer: Measure each signal in the computational basis and re-prepare the outcome. The decoded average is \(\frac34\ket0\bra0+\frac14\ket1\bra1=\rho\), exactly the source average, yet each individual signal is recovered with fidelity \(\frac58\). The average matrix forgets which signal was sent, so preserving it says nothing about preserving signals. A faithful compressor must give high fidelity for each signal (averaged over the ensemble), or equivalently preserve entanglement with a reference that purifies \(\rho\).

12-quantum-compression.question: No \(K\)-dimensional subspace can capture more weight of a state than the sum of its \(K\) largest eigenvalues (a result known as Ky Fan’s principle). (a) For \(\rho^{\otimes3}\) with eigenvalues \(\frac34,\frac14\), compute the best weight for \(K=2\) and \(K=4\). (b) Use the typical-string count to argue that for rates below \(S\), the best weight tends to zero as \(n\) grows.
hints: The eight eigenvalues are \(\frac{27}{64}\), three of \(\frac{9}{64}\), three of \(\frac{3}{64}\), and \(\frac1{64}\).
A typical string has eigenvalue about \(2^{-nS}\).
12-quantum-compression.answer: (a) \(K=2\): \(\frac{27+9}{64}=0.5625\). \(K=4\): \(\frac{27+27}{64}=0.844\), which the toy compressor attains. (b) With rate \(R<S\), the subspace has dimension \(K=2^{nR}\). Almost all weight lies on typical strings, each with eigenvalue about \(2^{-nS}\), so \(K\) of them carry at most about \(2^{nR}\cdot2^{-nS}=2^{-n(S-R)}\), which tends to zero; the atypical strings carry vanishing weight in total. So every encoding into fewer than \(nS\) qubits eventually loses almost all of the signal, which is the converse of Schumacher’s theorem in outline.

12-quantum-compression.question: The three-signal toy compressor uses \(2\) qubits for \(3\) signals, a rate of \(\frac23\), below \(S\approx0.811\), yet it achieves fidelity about \(0.78\). Does this contradict the converse of Schumacher’s theorem? Explain what happens at rate \(\frac23\) as \(n\) increases, and what changes at a rate above \(S\).
hints: The converse is a statement about the limit \(n\to\infty\).
At a fixed rate below \(S\), retained weight behaves like \(2^{-n(S-R)}\).
12-quantum-compression.answer: No. The theorem says that at any fixed rate below \(S\), fidelity cannot approach \(1\) as \(n\) grows; it allows imperfect fidelity for a short block. At rate \(\frac23\), the best retained weight shrinks roughly like \(2^{-n(0.811-0.667)}=2^{-0.14n}\) for large \(n\), so longer blocks make things worse, not better. Above \(S\), say at \(0.85\), the typical subspace eventually fits, and the fidelity approaches \(1\). Finite examples illustrate a theorem but cannot confirm or refute an asymptotic rate.

13-entanglement-transformations.question: Using the two-coefficient majorization rule, decide which conversions are possible deterministically by LOCC: (a) Schmidt probabilities \((0.6,0.4)\to(0.8,0.2)\); (b) \((0.8,0.2)\to(0.6,0.4)\); (c) \((1,0)\to(0.99,0.01)\).
hints: \(\psi\to\phi\) is possible when the largest coefficient of \(\psi\) is at most that of \(\phi\).
\((1,0)\) is a product state.
13-entanglement-transformations.answer: (a) Possible: \(0.6\le0.8\); the output is less entangled. (b) Impossible deterministically: \(0.8\le0.6\) fails, since it would increase entanglement. (c) Impossible: \(1\le0.99\) fails, because LOCC cannot create entanglement from a product state, even a tiny amount. Deterministic LOCC can only move toward less entangled states in this two-coefficient family.

13-entanglement-transformations.question: Find the Schmidt probabilities and the entanglement entropy of \(\frac{1}{\sqrt3}(\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{11})\), using its reduced state.
hints: The Schmidt probabilities are the eigenvalues of \(\rho_A=\begin{pmatrix}2/3&1/3\\1/3&1/3\end{pmatrix}\).
Trace \(1\), determinant \(\frac19\).
13-entanglement-transformations.answer: The eigenvalues of \(\rho_A\) are \(\frac12(1\pm\sqrt5/3)\approx0.873,0.127\). These are the Schmidt probabilities: in suitable local bases the state is \(\sqrt{0.873}\ket{u_0}\ket{v_0}+\sqrt{0.127}\ket{u_1}\ket{v_1}\). The entanglement entropy is \(h_2(0.873)\approx0.55\) ebits. Three nonzero amplitudes in the computational basis do not mean three Schmidt terms: a two-qubit pure state always has at most two.

13-entanglement-transformations.question: For the one-copy filter on \(\sqrt p\ket{00}+\sqrt{1-p}\ket{11}\), compute the success probability \(2(1-p)\) and the expected ebit yield for \(p=0.6\) and \(p=0.9\), and compare each with the entanglement entropy \(h_2(p)\).
hints: On success the output is one Bell pair; on failure a product state.
13-entanglement-transformations.answer: For \(p=0.6\): success \(0.8\), expected yield \(0.8\) ebit, against \(h_2(0.6)\approx0.971\). For \(p=0.9\): success \(0.2\), yield \(0.2\), against \(0.469\). In both cases the expected yield is below the entropy, as it must be: LOCC cannot increase entanglement on average. The single-copy filter is closest to optimal when the state is already nearly maximally entangled.

13-entanglement-transformations.question: Generalize the filter to a partially entangled target. Starting from \(\sqrt p\ket{00}+\sqrt{1-p}\ket{11}\) with \(p\ge\frac12\), Alice applies \(K=\mathrm{diag}(a,1)\) to obtain \(\sqrt q\ket{00}+\sqrt{1-q}\ket{11}\) with \(\frac12\le q<p\). (a) Find \(a\). (b) Show that the success probability is \(\frac{1-p}{1-q}\). (c) Check the case \(q=\frac12\), and explain why \(q>p\) needs no filter.
hints: The output amplitudes must be in the ratio \(\sqrt q:\sqrt{1-q}\).
Success probability is \(a^2p+(1-p)\).
13-entanglement-transformations.answer: (a) The output is \(a\sqrt p\ket{00}+\sqrt{1-p}\ket{11}\); requiring \(a\sqrt p/\sqrt{1-p}=\sqrt{q/(1-q)}\) gives \(a=\sqrt{\frac{q(1-p)}{p(1-q)}}\le1\), so \(K\) is a valid filter. (b) Success probability \(a^2p+(1-p)=\frac{q(1-p)}{1-q}+(1-p)=\frac{1-p}{1-q}\). (c) For \(q=\frac12\) this is \(2(1-p)\), the Bell-pair filter. For \(q>p\) the target is less entangled, so majorization allows a deterministic conversion. This success probability is known to be optimal for two-coefficient states (Vidal’s theorem).

13-entanglement-transformations.question: Alice and Bob hold two copies of \(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\ket{00}+\frac12\ket{11}\). Alice measures how many \(1\)s her two-qubit label contains (\(0\), \(1\), or \(2\)) without distinguishing which positions. (a) Find each outcome’s probability and the resulting state. (b) Compute the expected ebits per copy and compare with the one-copy filter and with \(h_2(\frac14)\).
hints: The joint state is \(\frac34\ket{00,00}+\frac{\sqrt3}{4}(\ket{01,01}+\ket{10,10})+\frac14\ket{11,11}\), pairing Alice’s and Bob’s labels.
Outcome “one \(1\)” keeps two terms with equal amplitude.
13-entanglement-transformations.answer: (a) “Zero 1s”: probability \(\frac9{16}\), leaving the product \(\ket{00}\ket{00}\). “Two 1s”: \(\frac1{16}\), leaving \(\ket{11}\ket{11}\). “One 1”: \(\frac{6}{16}\), leaving \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{01}\ket{01}+\ket{10}\ket{10})\), a maximally entangled state of a two-dimensional subspace, worth one ebit. (b) The yield is \(\frac{6}{16}\) ebit per two copies, \(0.19\) per copy, worse than the one-copy filter’s \(0.5\) and far from \(0.811\). Measuring the number of \(1\)s is the start of the asymptotically optimal concentration protocol, but its advantage appears only for many copies, where the equal-weight blocks become large.

13-entanglement-transformations.question: Consider \(\rho_p=(1-p)\ket{\Phi^+}\bra{\Phi^+}+pI/4\). (a) Using the partial transpose of \(\ket{\Phi^+}\bra{\Phi^+}\) found when testing complete positivity (eigenvalues \(\frac12,\frac12,\frac12,-\frac12\)), find the eigenvalues of the partial transpose of \(\rho_p\). (b) For which \(p\) is one of them negative? (c) For two qubits, a state is separable exactly when its partial transpose has no negative eigenvalue (a cited theorem). For which \(p\) is \(\rho_p\) entangled?
hints: The partial transpose of \(I/4\) is \(I/4\).
The eigenvectors of the two parts can be chosen in common.
13-entanglement-transformations.answer: (a) The partial transpose is \((1-p)\Gamma+\frac p4I\), where \(\Gamma\) has eigenvalues \(\pm\frac12\), so the eigenvalues are \(\frac{1-p}{2}+\frac p4\) (three times) and \(-\frac{1-p}{2}+\frac p4\). (b) The last is negative when \(\frac p4<\frac{1-p}{2}\), that is, \(p<\frac23\). (c) So \(\rho_p\) is entangled for \(p<\frac23\) and separable for \(p\ge\frac23\). At \(p=\frac23\), with fidelity \(\frac12\) to \(\ket{\Phi^+}\), enough white noise has been added to make the state preparable by local operations and shared randomness.

13-entanglement-transformations.question: Explain how Alice and Bob can create \(n\) copies of \(\sqrt p\ket{00}+\sqrt{1-p}\ket{11}\) using about \(nh_2(p)\) Bell pairs and classical communication. Use Schumacher compression and teleportation. What fidelity guarantee does the procedure have, and why is it not exact?
hints: Alice can prepare all \(2n\) qubits locally, then send Bob his halves.
Bob’s halves have average state with entropy \(h_2(p)\).
13-entanglement-transformations.answer: Alice prepares the \(n\) copies entirely in her laboratory. Bob’s \(n\) halves have reduced state \(\rho^{\otimes n}\) with \(S(\rho)=h_2(p)\), so Schumacher compression fits them into about \(nh_2(p)\) qubits while preserving their entanglement with Alice’s halves. She teleports the compressed qubits, consuming one Bell pair and two classical bits each, and Bob decompresses. The result approximates the \(n\) copies with fidelity approaching \(1\) as \(n\) grows, not exactly, because compression discards the atypical subspace. This is entanglement dilution at rate \(h_2(p)\), matching the concentration rate.

13-entanglement-transformations.question: A student argues: “Entanglement entropy ranks pure states, so a state with more entropy can always be converted deterministically into one with less.” Test the claim with three-term Schmidt vectors \(\psi=(0.4,0.4,0.2)\) and \(\phi=(0.5,0.25,0.25)\) on qutrits.
hints: Compute the entropies, then compare the partial sums of the sorted coefficients.
Check both directions.
13-entanglement-transformations.answer: \(S(\psi)\approx1.522\) and \(S(\phi)=1.5\), so \(\psi\) has more entropy. Deterministic conversion \(\psi\to\phi\) requires each partial sum of \(\psi\) to be at most that of \(\phi\): \(0.4\le0.5\) holds, but \(0.8\le0.75\) fails. The reverse also fails, since \(0.5\le0.4\) is false. Neither state can be converted into the other with certainty, despite their different entropies. For single copies, majorization is only a partial order; the entropy ordering becomes decisive only for asymptotic conversions with many copies.

13-entanglement-transformations.question: A catalyst is an entangled state that is used and returned unchanged. Let \(\psi=(0.4,0.4,0.1,0.1)\), \(\phi=(0.5,0.25,0.25,0)\), and the catalyst \(c=(0.6,0.4)\). (a) Show that \(\psi\to\phi\) is impossible deterministically. (b) Compute the sorted coefficients of \(\psi\otimes c\) and \(\phi\otimes c\) and show that \(\psi\otimes c\to\phi\otimes c\) satisfies majorization. (c) Interpret the result.
13-entanglement-transformations.answer: (a) The second partial sums give \(0.8\le0.75\), which fails. (b) \(\psi\otimes c\) sorted: \(0.24,0.24,0.16,0.16,0.06,0.06,0.04,0.04\), with partial sums \(0.24,0.48,0.64,0.80,0.86,0.92,0.96,1\). \(\phi\otimes c\) sorted: \(0.30,0.20,0.15,0.15,0.10,0.10,0,0\), with partial sums \(0.30,0.50,0.65,0.80,0.90,1,1,1\). Every partial sum of the first is at most the corresponding one of the second, so the conversion is allowed. (c) With the catalyst present, Alice and Bob can convert \(\psi\) to \(\phi\) deterministically and get the catalyst back intact. This example is due to Jonathan and Plenio (1999); it shows that single-copy entanglement theory depends on which auxiliary resources are allowed.

13-entanglement-transformations.question: For the classically correlated state \(\rho_c=\frac12(\ket{00}\bra{00}+\ket{11}\bra{11})\) and for \(\ket{\Phi^+}\), state the entanglement cost and the distillable entanglement. Then explain why, starting from \(\ket{\Phi^+}\) and allowing Bob to discard a phase record, the conversion \(\ket{\Phi^+}\to\rho_c\) is easy by LOCC while \(\rho_c\to\ket{\Phi^+}\) is impossible.
hints: \(\rho_c\) is separable.
LOCC cannot create entanglement from separable states.
13-entanglement-transformations.answer: \(\rho_c\) is separable: Alice flips a fair coin, tells Bob the value, and both prepare it, so its entanglement cost and distillable entanglement are both \(0\). A Bell pair costs \(1\) ebit and yields \(1\) ebit. Converting \(\ket{\Phi^+}\) to \(\rho_c\) needs only that one party measure in \(Z\) and discard the result (or dephase locally), which LOCC allows. The reverse would create entanglement from a separable state, which LOCC cannot do: classical messages and local operations map mixtures of products to mixtures of products. The lost coherence went into a record that the protocol does not allow them to recover.

14-quantum-error-correction.question: For the three-qubit bit-flip code, give the syndrome \((Z_1Z_2,Z_2Z_3)\) after (a) \(X_3\) and (b) \(X_1X_3\). What does the standard decoder do in case (b), and what is the net effect?
hints: A parity is \(-\) when its two bits disagree.
14-quantum-error-correction.answer: (a) \(X_3\) gives \(\alpha\ket{001}+\beta\ket{110}\): \(Z_1Z_2=+\), \(Z_2Z_3=-\). (b) \(X_1X_3\) gives \(\alpha\ket{101}+\beta\ket{010}\): both parities are \(-\), the syndrome of a single \(X_2\). The decoder applies \(X_2\), so the total is \(X_1X_2X_3\), which exchanges \(\ket{000}\) and \(\ket{111}\): a logical bit flip \((\alpha,\beta)\to(\beta,\alpha)\) with no warning. Any two flips are decoded into a logical error.

14-quantum-error-correction.question: Encode \(\ket+\) as \((\ket{000}+\ket{111})/\sqrt2\). Find the reduced state of physical qubit \(1\). Could a measurement on that one qubit reveal whether the logical state was \(\ket{+}\) or \(\ket-\)?
hints: Tracing out qubits \(2,3\) removes the cross terms because their labels \(00\) and \(11\) differ.
Encode \(\ket-\) and compare.
14-quantum-error-correction.answer: Qubit \(1\) has reduced state \(\mathrm{diag}(\frac12,\frac12)=I/2\): the cross terms vanish because the other two qubits carry orthogonal labels. Encoding \(\ket-\) gives \((\ket{000}-\ket{111})/\sqrt2\), whose single-qubit reductions are also \(I/2\). No measurement on one physical qubit distinguishes them. The logical phase lives only in the joint state, which is why a local error on one qubit cannot read it, and also why a single-qubit phase error can still change it.

14-quantum-error-correction.question: The phase-flip code encodes \(\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\) as \(\alpha\ket{+++}+\beta\ket{---}\). What does \(Z_2\) do to the encoded state? Which parities, \(X_1X_2\) and \(X_2X_3\), detect it, and with what results?
hints: \(Z\ket\pm=\ket\mp\).
\(X\) has eigenvalue \(+1\) on \(\ket+\) and \(-1\) on \(\ket-\).
14-quantum-error-correction.answer: \(Z_2\) gives \(\alpha\ket{+-+}+\beta\ket{-+-}\). In the \(\pm\) labels this is exactly a “bit flip” on the middle position, so both \(X_1X_2\) and \(X_2X_3\) return \(-1\), in both branches, without revealing \(\alpha,\beta\). The phase-flip code is the bit-flip code written in the \(\pm\) basis: it corrects single \(Z\) errors.

14-quantum-error-correction.question: Measure the parity \(Z_1Z_2\) of \(\alpha\ket{010}+\beta\ket{101}\) by computing \(q_1\oplus q_2\) into an ancilla \(\ket0\) with two CNOTs. (a) Write the joint state after the CNOTs. (b) Is the ancilla entangled with the data? (c) Compare with measuring qubit \(1\) directly.
hints: In both branches, \(q_1\oplus q_2=1\).
A direct measurement of qubit \(1\) gives \(0\) in one branch and \(1\) in the other.
14-quantum-error-correction.answer: (a) Both terms have \(q_1\oplus q_2=1\), so the state becomes \((\alpha\ket{010}+\beta\ket{101})\otimes\ket1\). (b) The ancilla is in a product with the data: measuring it gives \(1\) with certainty and leaves the logical superposition untouched. (c) Measuring qubit \(1\) directly would give \(0\) (from the \(\alpha\) branch) or \(1\) (from the \(\beta\) branch) with probabilities \(|\alpha|^2,|\beta|^2\), collapsing the encoded qubit. The parity is the same for both branches, so learning it learns about the error and nothing about the logical state.

14-quantum-error-correction.question: Each physical qubit independently suffers \(X\) with probability \(p\). After ideal syndrome measurement and correction, the logical qubit undergoes \(X_L\) with probability \(p_L\). (a) Show \(p_L=3p^2-2p^3\). (b) Write the resulting logical channel. (c) Evaluate at \(p=0.01\) and \(p=0.1\), and find the value of \(p\) above which encoding hurts.
hints: A logical error occurs when two or three qubits flip.
Compare \(3p^2-2p^3\) with \(p\).
14-quantum-error-correction.answer: (a) Two flips occur with probability \(3p^2(1-p)\) and three with \(p^3\); both lead to \(X_L\), giving \(3p^2-2p^3\). (b) The logical channel is \(\rho_L\mapsto(1-p_L)\rho_L+p_LX_L\rho_LX_L\), a bit-flip channel with a smaller probability. (c) At \(p=0.01\), \(p_L\approx3.0\times10^{-4}\); at \(p=0.1\), \(p_L=0.028\). Encoding helps when \(3p^2-2p^3<p\), that is \(p<\frac12\). These figures assume perfect syndrome measurement and recovery and pure bit-flip noise.

14-quantum-error-correction.question: Use the Knill–Laflamme condition \(PE_a^\dagger E_bP=c_{ab}P\) with \(P=\ket{000}\bra{000}+\ket{111}\bra{111}\). (a) Show that the error set \(\{I,Z_1Z_2\}\) satisfies it. (b) What does \(Z_1Z_2\) do to a codeword, and does it need correcting? (c) Contrast with \(\{I,Z_1\}\).
hints: \(Z_1Z_2\) has eigenvalue \(+1\) on both \(\ket{000}\) and \(\ket{111}\).
14-quantum-error-correction.answer: (a) \(Z_1Z_2\ket{000}=\ket{000}\) and \(Z_1Z_2\ket{111}=\ket{111}\), so \(PZ_1Z_2P=P\) and every pair satisfies the condition, with \(c_{ab}=1\). (b) \(Z_1Z_2\) acts as the identity on the code space, so it needs no correction at all: the logical qubit is unaffected. (c) \(PZ_1P=\ket{000}\bra{000}-\ket{111}\bra{111}\) is not a multiple of \(P\), so \(\{I,Z_1\}\) fails: \(Z_1\) acts as the logical \(Z\), and no recovery can tell whether it happened. Some physical errors are harmless to a code, and the condition recognizes them.

14-quantum-error-correction.question: Apply \(X_1\) to the phase-flip-code state \(\alpha\ket{+++}+\beta\ket{---}\). (a) What is the new state? (b) Do the syndromes \(X_1X_2\), \(X_2X_3\) detect it? (c) What logical operation has occurred, and what does this say about protecting against both kinds of error?
hints: \(X\ket+=\ket+\) and \(X\ket-=-\ket-\).
The \(X\) parities are unchanged by a sign.
14-quantum-error-correction.answer: (a) \(X_1\) gives \(\alpha\ket{+++}-\beta\ket{---}\). (b) The parities \(X_1X_2\), \(X_2X_3\) are still \(+1\) in both branches: the error is invisible. (c) It is a logical \(Z\), changing \(\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1\) to \(\alpha\ket0-\beta\ket1\). Each three-qubit code corrects one kind of single-qubit error and is defenseless against the other. Protecting against arbitrary single-qubit errors requires a code that detects both, such as Shor’s nine-qubit code, which nests the two repetition codes.

14-quantum-error-correction.question: A student objects: “Measuring \(Z_1Z_2\) and \(Z_2Z_3\) is a measurement of the encoded qubit, so it must collapse \(\alpha\ket{000}+\beta\ket{111}\) and destroy the superposition.” Take \(\alpha=\beta=1/\sqrt2\) and the error \(X_1\). Compute the syndrome probabilities and the state afterward.
hints: Both terms have the same parity values.
14-quantum-error-correction.answer: After \(X_1\) the state is \((\ket{100}+\ket{011})/\sqrt2\). Both terms have \(Z_1Z_2=-1\) and \(Z_2Z_3=+1\), so the syndrome is \((-,+)\) with probability \(1\), and the measurement leaves the state unchanged. Applying \(X_1\) then restores \((\ket{000}+\ket{111})/\sqrt2\) exactly. The syndrome observables have the same value on every codeword (and on every codeword with the same error), so they distinguish error subspaces and nothing within them. A measurement collapses only the distinctions it resolves.

14-quantum-error-correction.question: Concatenate the bit-flip code: encode each of the three physical qubits again with the same code (nine qubits), and correct at both levels. For small \(p\), use \(p_L\approx3p^2\) at each level. (a) Estimate the second-level logical error probability. (b) Evaluate for \(p=0.01\). (c) For which \(p\) does concatenation keep reducing the error, under this approximation, and what assumptions make the estimate optimistic?
hints: The second level sees each first-level block as a qubit with error \(3p^2\).
Iterating \(p\mapsto3p^2\) shrinks \(p\) when \(3p<1\).
14-quantum-error-correction.answer: (a) Each level-one block fails with probability about \(3p^2\), and the level-two code fails when two of its three blocks fail: \(3(3p^2)^2=27p^4\). (b) At \(p=0.01\): level one gives \(3\times10^{-4}\), level two \(2.7\times10^{-7}\). (c) Iterating \(p\mapsto3p^2\) decreases the error when \(p<\frac13\) in this approximation: a threshold. The estimate assumes independent bit-flip noise only, perfect syndrome measurement, and perfect correction gates. Real fault-tolerant thresholds are much lower, because the recovery circuits themselves introduce errors.

14-quantum-error-correction.question: A code storing one logical qubit in \(n\) physical qubits corrects every single-qubit error (\(X\), \(Y\), or \(Z\) on any qubit) and maps each such error, and the no-error case, to its own orthogonal two-dimensional subspace. (a) Show that this requires \(2(1+3n)\le2^n\). (b) Find the smallest \(n\). (c) What is special about that value, and why can the three-qubit codes not satisfy the bound?
hints: Count the distinct error cases: no error plus three Paulis on each of \(n\) qubits.
The orthogonal subspaces must fit in the \(2^n\)-dimensional space.
14-quantum-error-correction.answer: (a) There are \(1+3n\) cases, each requiring an orthogonal two-dimensional subspace, so \(2(1+3n)\le2^n\). (b) \(n=3\): \(20>8\); \(n=4\): \(26>16\); \(n=5\): \(32\le32\). So \(n\ge5\). (c) At \(n=5\) the bound is met with equality: the subspaces fill the whole space, and the five-qubit code achieves this, so it is called perfect. Three qubits have room for only four orthogonal two-dimensional subspaces, enough for no error and three bit flips, but not for phase errors as well. (Degenerate codes, in which different errors act identically on the code, are not covered by this counting.)

15-quantum-communication.question: Using \(C=1-e\), \(C_E=2(1-e)\), and \(Q=\max(0,1-2e)\) for the qubit erasure channel, evaluate all three at \(e=0.1\) and \(e=\frac12\). What is special about \(e=\frac12\)?
hints: Substitute directly.
Compare \(Q\) with \(C\) at each value.
15-quantum-communication.answer: At \(e=0.1\): \(C=0.9\) bits, \(C_E=1.8\) bits, \(Q=0.8\) qubits per use. At \(e=\frac12\): \(C=0.5\), \(C_E=1\), \(Q=0\). At \(e=\frac12\) the channel can still carry classical information, and even more with shared entanglement, yet it cannot carry quantum information at any positive rate without assistance. Quantum transmission is the most demanding of the three tasks.

15-quantum-communication.question: Which kind of transmission does each task require? (a) Sending the result of a measurement; (b) sending half of a Bell pair so that Alice and Bob share entanglement; (c) transferring an unknown qubit using a pre-shared Bell pair. Name the resources each consumes.
hints: Ask whether the receiver must identify a label or preserve coherence with a reference.
Teleportation needs classical messages and an ebit.
15-quantum-communication.answer: (a) Classical: the receiver must identify a label, so a measure-and-resend channel would suffice. (b) Quantum: the transmitted qubit must stay coherent with Alice’s half, so the channel must preserve entanglement, which is exactly what quantum capacity measures. (c) Classical, with entanglement assistance: two classical bits per qubit and one ebit, with no quantum channel used during the protocol. The same physical outcome, a qubit at Bob, can be achieved with very different resource accounts.

15-quantum-communication.question: A team reports sending \(900\) message bits reliably over \(1000\) uses of an erasure channel with \(e=0.25\). Another reports \(700\). Which claim is consistent with the capacity, and what must the reported rate count?
hints: Rate is message bits divided by all channel uses.
15-quantum-communication.answer: The capacity is \(0.75\) bits per use, so \(900\) bits in \(1000\) uses (rate \(0.9\)) cannot be sent reliably without some other resource, while \(700\) (rate \(0.7\)) is below capacity and plausible for a good code. The rate must count all channel uses, erased ones included; dividing by the \(750\) or so successful positions would overstate it. A claim above capacity signals an error or an unaccounted resource, such as feedback or shared entanglement.

15-quantum-communication.question: The dephasing channel applies \(Z\) with probability \(p\). (a) Show that its classical capacity is \(1\) bit per use, using inputs \(\ket0,\ket1\). (b) Send half of \(\ket{\Phi^+}\) through it and compute \(S(B)\), \(S(RB)\), and the coherent information. (c) Evaluate at \(p=0.1\). (The quantum capacity of this channel equals the single-use value found in (b).)
hints: \(Z\) leaves \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\) unchanged.
The output joint state is \((1-p)\ket{\Phi^+}\bra{\Phi^+}+p\ket{\Phi^-}\bra{\Phi^-}\).
15-quantum-communication.answer: (a) \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\) pass unchanged, so one bit per use is sent perfectly, and a qubit cannot carry more than one bit. (b) Bob’s output is \(I/2\), so \(S(B)=1\). The joint output is \((1-p)\ket{\Phi^+}\bra{\Phi^+}+p\ket{\Phi^-}\bra{\Phi^-}\), with eigenvalues \(1-p,p\), so \(S(RB)=h_2(p)\). The coherent information is \(1-h_2(p)\). (c) At \(p=0.1\), about \(0.531\) qubits per use. Phase noise is harmless for classical bits in the computational basis but costs quantum capacity, because it damages coherence.

15-quantum-communication.question: Send a classical bit over the erasure channel by repetition: transmit it \(r\) times and decode from any unerased copy. (a) Find the failure probability and rate. (b) Evaluate for \(r=3\) and \(e=\frac14\). (c) Compare the rate with the capacity \(1-e\), and describe a better strategy that uses the receiver’s knowledge of erasures.
hints: Failure means all \(r\) copies are erased.
Long block codes for erasures can approach rate \(1-e\).
15-quantum-communication.answer: (a) Failure requires every copy to be erased: probability \(e^r\), at rate \(1/r\). (b) For \(r=3\), \(e=\frac14\): failure \(\frac{1}{64}\approx0.016\) at rate \(\frac13\). (c) The capacity is \(0.75\), more than twice that rate. Because Bob knows which positions were erased, a long code needs only enough redundancy to fill in the missing fraction, about \(e\) of the positions, approaching rate \(1-e\) with vanishing error. Repetition wastes the information already carried by the unerased uses.

15-quantum-communication.question: Show that dense coding achieves the entanglement-assisted rate \(2(1-e)\) on the erasure channel. (a) What happens to each dense-coded qubit when it is erased and when it is not? (b) Combine with an outer classical erasure code to find the rate. (c) Evaluate at \(e=\frac14\) and compare with \(C=\frac34\).
hints: A successful use delivers both bits; an erasure delivers a flag.
The receiver knows which uses were erased.
15-quantum-communication.answer: (a) If the qubit arrives, Bob holds both halves of the encoded Bell state and decodes two bits exactly; if it is erased, he gets the flag and learns nothing, but knows the two bits are missing. (b) Each use is a two-bit symbol erasure channel with erasure probability \(e\), and an outer erasure code over these symbols approaches rate \(2(1-e)\) bits per use. (c) At \(e=\frac14\), \(1.5\) bits per use, twice the unassisted \(0.75\). The extra bit is paid for by one ebit per use, distributed in advance.

15-quantum-communication.question: With free two-way classical communication, Alice can send halves of Bell pairs through an erasure channel, learn from Bob which arrived, keep only those pairs, and then teleport her qubits. (a) What rate of qubits per channel use does this give? (b) Compare with \(Q=\max(0,1-2e)\) at \(e=\frac14\) and \(e=\frac34\). (c) Why is this not a contradiction?
hints: A fraction \(1-e\) of Bell halves arrive intact.
Teleportation needs only classical messages once the pairs are shared.
15-quantum-communication.answer: (a) On average \(1-e\) pairs per use survive, and each teleports one qubit using classical messages, so the rate is \(1-e\) qubits per use. (b) At \(e=\frac14\): \(0.75\) against \(Q=0.5\); at \(e=\frac34\): \(0.25\) against \(Q=0\). (c) The unassisted capacity forbids classical feedback, and without it Alice does not know which uses failed, so she must protect every qubit in advance. Feedback lets her discard failures after the fact. Capacities depend on the assistance allowed and must be compared under the same resource model.

15-quantum-communication.question: A student argues: “On an erasure channel with \(e=\frac14\), three quarters of the qubits arrive perfectly, so the quantum capacity is \(\frac34\).” Explain why the unassisted quantum capacity is only \(\frac12\), identifying what Alice does not know when she encodes.
hints: Without feedback, Alice must choose the encoding before knowing which positions will be erased.
Compare with the classical capacity, which is \(\frac34\).
15-quantum-communication.answer: The \(\frac34\) counts successful positions after the fact. Alice must encode an unknown quantum state before transmission, without knowing which positions will be erased, and the encoding cannot copy her state onto several positions (no-cloning). It must spread the state so that any typical subset of \(\frac34\) of the positions suffices, while the erased \(\frac14\) reveal nothing. The coding theorem shows this works only up to \(1-2e=\frac12\). Classical bits can be repeated freely, so the classical capacity reaches \(\frac34\); quantum information cannot.

15-quantum-communication.question: Use no-cloning to show that the erasure channel with \(e=\frac12\) has zero quantum capacity. Model the channel as an isometry that sends the input to Bob with probability \(\frac12\) and to the environment otherwise, each time leaving the other party a flag. Argue that a code allowing Bob to recover the quantum message would also let the environment recover it.
hints: At \(e=\frac12\) the roles of Bob and the environment are symmetric.
Two parties each holding a decodable copy of an unknown state would amount to cloning.
15-quantum-communication.answer: At \(e=\frac12\), each use delivers the input to Bob or to the environment with equal probability, and whoever does not receive it gets a flag: the channel to Bob and the channel to the environment are identical. If some code let Bob reconstruct an unknown quantum message with fidelity near \(1\), the same decoder applied by the environment to its outputs would also reconstruct it. Together they would produce two copies of an unknown state, which no-cloning forbids. So no positive rate is possible at \(e=\frac12\), and by degrading the channel further, none for \(e>\frac12\) either, consistent with \(Q=\max(0,1-2e)\).

15-quantum-communication.question: For amplitude damping with parameter \(\gamma\) and the maximally mixed input (half of \(\ket{\Phi^+}\)), (a) find Bob’s output and \(S(B)\); (b) argue that \(S(RB)\) equals the entropy of the environment, which receives the excitation with probability \(\gamma/2\); (c) compute the coherent information \(h_2\big(\frac{1-\gamma}{2}\big)-h_2\big(\frac\gamma2\big)\) for \(\gamma=0.2\) and \(\gamma=0.5\).
hints: The output of \(I/2\) is \(\mathrm{diag}\big(\frac{1+\gamma}{2},\frac{1-\gamma}{2}\big)\).
The total state of \(R\), \(B\), and the environment is pure, so \(S(RB)=S(E)\).
15-quantum-communication.answer: (a) Amplitude damping maps \(I/2\) to \(\mathrm{diag}\big(\frac{1+\gamma}{2},\frac{1-\gamma}{2}\big)\), so \(S(B)=h_2\big(\frac{1-\gamma}{2}\big)\). (b) Modelling the channel as a unitary with an environment in \(\ket0\), the joint state of \(R\), \(B\), and \(E\) is pure, so \(S(RB)=S(E)\). The environment ends in \(\ket1\) exactly when a decay occurs, which happens with probability \(\gamma\cdot\frac12\), so \(S(E)=h_2(\gamma/2)\). (c) For \(\gamma=0.2\): \(h_2(0.4)-h_2(0.1)\approx0.971-0.469=0.502\). For \(\gamma=0.5\): \(h_2(0.25)-h_2(0.25)=0\). With this input, coherent information vanishes once the environment learns as much as Bob; the quantum capacity of amplitude damping is in fact zero for \(\gamma\ge\frac12\).

16-quantum-cryptography.question: In BB84, Alice and Bob each choose the \(Z\) basis with probability \(0.9\) and the \(X\) basis with probability \(0.1\), independently. What fraction of rounds is sifted? Why might they prefer this to fair basis choices, and what must they still be able to do with the rarely used basis?
hints: Matching probability is \(0.9^2+0.1^2\).
Security relies on testing both bases.
16-quantum-cryptography.answer: Matching occurs with probability \(0.81+0.01=0.82\), compared with \(0.5\) for fair choices, so far fewer rounds are discarded. The \(X\) rounds are still essential: they are where an attack that measures in \(Z\) shows up as errors. With biased choices, Alice and Bob need enough \(X\)-basis data to estimate its error rate with the required confidence, which the analysis must account for.

16-quantum-cryptography.question: Evaluate the ideal asymptotic key rate \(1-2h_2(Q)\) per sifted bit for \(Q=0.02\) and \(Q=0.11\). What does the second value suggest about the tolerable error rate in this model?
16-quantum-cryptography.answer: At \(Q=0.02\): \(1-2(0.141)\approx0.717\) secret bits per sifted bit. At \(Q=0.11\): \(1-2(0.500)\approx0\). In this ideal one-way model, no key can be extracted once the error rate reaches about \(11\%\). Finite data, detector imperfections, and authentication costs reduce the usable rate and the tolerable error further.

16-quantum-cryptography.question: A sifted raw key of \(6\) uniformly random bits is reconciled by publishing the parities of the pairs \((1,2)\), \((3,4)\), and \((5,6)\). How many bits of uncertainty does Eve have left, assuming she knew nothing else? How long a secret key can be extracted?
hints: Each published parity removes one bit of uncertainty.
Choose one bit from each pair.
16-quantum-cryptography.answer: Each independent parity halves the possible strings, so Eve’s uncertainty falls from \(6\) bits to \(3\). Taking the first bit of each pair gives \(3\) bits that are uniform and independent of the published parities, so a \(3\)-bit key can be extracted. Every bit leaked in public reconciliation must be subtracted from the final key length.

16-quantum-cryptography.question: Eve intercepts every signal, always measures in \(Z\), and resends her result. (a) Find the error rate on sifted \(Z\) rounds and on sifted \(X\) rounds. (b) What is the average sifted error rate with fair basis choices? (c) How can Alice and Bob detect this attack more effectively than by the average alone, and how much does Eve learn?
hints: In \(Z\) rounds Eve’s measurement does not disturb the state.
In \(X\) rounds Bob receives a \(Z\) eigenstate and measures \(X\).
16-quantum-cryptography.answer: (a) On \(Z\) rounds Eve measures the right basis, resends the same state, and causes no error. On \(X\) rounds she resends \(\ket0\) or \(\ket1\), and Bob’s \(X\) measurement is a fair coin: error \(\frac12\). (b) The average is \(\frac14\), the same as the random-basis attack. (c) Estimating the error separately for each basis shows \(0\) in \(Z\) and \(\frac12\) in \(X\), a clear signature. Eve learns every \(Z\) key bit and nothing about \(X\) key bits. Basis-resolved error estimates constrain attacks more tightly than a single average.

16-quantum-cryptography.question: In an intercept-resend attack, Eve measures every signal in the intermediate basis \(\ket{b_0}=\cos\frac\pi8\ket0+\sin\frac\pi8\ket1\), \(\ket{b_1}=-\sin\frac\pi8\ket0+\cos\frac\pi8\ket1\), guessing bit \(0\) on \(b_0\), and resends the state she found. (a) For Alice’s \(\ket0\), find the probability that Eve guesses correctly and the error Bob sees in a \(Z\) measurement. (b) Compare with the random \(Z\)/\(X\) intercept-resend attack. (c) What does the comparison show?
hints: \(|\braket{b_0}0|^2=\cos^2\frac\pi8\approx0.854\).
Bob errs if Eve resends \(\ket{b_0}\) and he finds \(1\), or \(\ket{b_1}\) and he finds \(0\).
16-quantum-cryptography.answer: (a) Eve guesses correctly with probability \(\cos^2\frac\pi8\approx0.854\). Bob’s error is \(\cos^2\frac\pi8\sin^2\frac\pi8+\sin^2\frac\pi8\cos^2\frac\pi8=2(0.854)(0.146)=0.25\). The basis is equally inclined to \(Z\) and \(X\), so \(X\) rounds behave the same way. (b) The random-basis attack also causes \(25\%\) error, but Eve then guesses correctly only \(\frac12\cdot1+\frac12\cdot\frac12=75\%\) of the time. (c) For the same disturbance, a cleverer measurement gives Eve more information. Security proofs must bound what any attack can learn for a given error, not analyse one convenient attack.

16-quantum-cryptography.question: Alice and Bob test \(n=100\) randomly chosen sifted bits and find no errors. (a) If the true error rate is \(Q\), what is the probability of seeing no errors? (b) What is the largest \(Q\) that remains consistent with this observation if they accept a failure probability of \(10^{-3}\)? (c) What must the security analysis use in place of “\(Q=0\)”?
hints: \(P(\text{no errors})=(1-Q)^n\).
16-quantum-cryptography.answer: (a) \((1-Q)^{100}\). (b) Setting \((1-Q)^{100}=10^{-3}\) gives \(Q=1-10^{-0.03}\approx0.067\). Any error rate up to about \(6.7\%\) could produce zero observed errors with probability at least \(10^{-3}\). (c) The analysis must use this upper bound (or a sharper one), together with its failure probability, as the error parameter. With \(Q\approx6.7\%\), the ideal key rate is \(1-2h_2(0.067)\approx0.29\) instead of \(1\). Finite data costs key length even when nothing goes wrong.

16-quantum-cryptography.question: A raw key \(x_1x_2x_3x_4\) is uniformly random, and Eve has learned only the parity \(x_1\oplus x_2\). (a) Show that \(x_1\) is uniform and independent of Eve’s information. (b) Give a \(3\)-bit key that is perfectly secret, and explain why \((x_1,x_2,x_3)\) would not be. (c) How does this illustrate privacy amplification?
hints: For each value of the parity, \(x_1\) is still \(0\) or \(1\) with equal probability.
\(x_2=x_1\oplus(x_1\oplus x_2)\).
16-quantum-cryptography.answer: (a) For either value of \(x_1\oplus x_2\), there are two equally likely pairs, one with \(x_1=0\) and one with \(x_1=1\), so \(x_1\) is uniform and independent of the parity. (b) \((x_1,x_3,x_4)\) is uniform and independent of what Eve knows, so it is perfectly secret. \((x_1,x_2,x_3)\) is not: Eve can compute \(x_1\oplus x_2\) from it, so only \(8/2=4\) of its \(8\) values are possible given her knowledge. (c) Privacy amplification maps the raw key to a shorter string chosen to be independent of the adversary’s information; when Eve knows \(k\) independent parities of an \(n\)-bit uniform key, \(n-k\) secret bits can be extracted. Quantum security proofs supply the corresponding bound when Eve holds quantum information.

16-quantum-cryptography.question: A student claims: “BB84 is secured by physics, so Alice and Bob do not need an authenticated classical channel.” Describe an attack by an adversary who controls both the quantum channel and an unauthenticated classical channel, and explain what authentication provides.
hints: Can Eve pretend to be Bob to Alice and Alice to Bob?
No-cloning protects the quantum signals only against an outsider.
16-quantum-cryptography.answer: Eve runs one BB84 session with Alice, pretending to be Bob, and another with Bob, pretending to be Alice, using the unauthenticated channel to answer each party’s basis announcements and tests. Each session shows no disturbance, because Eve is a legitimate endpoint in each. She ends up with one key shared with Alice and another with Bob, and can read and re-encrypt every message. The quantum part guarantees only that an outsider cannot learn a key without causing errors; authentication guarantees that the outsider is not the other endpoint. It requires a short pre-shared secret, so QKD expands a shared key rather than creating one from nothing.

16-quantum-cryptography.question: In the entanglement-based description, suppose Eve copies the \(Z\) value of the photon in transit with a CNOT onto her own qubit, so that Alice, Bob, and Eve share \((\ket{000}+\ket{111})/\sqrt2\). (a) What error rate do Alice and Bob see in \(Z\) rounds, and what does Eve know? (b) Compute \(\langle X_AX_B\rangle\) for this state, and the error rate in \(X\) rounds. (c) What principle does the result illustrate?
hints: An \(X\)-round error means Alice’s and Bob’s \(\pm\) results differ.
16-quantum-cryptography.answer: (a) In \(Z\) rounds the three outcomes always agree: no error, and Eve knows every \(Z\) bit. (b) \(X_AX_B\ket{000}=\ket{110}\) and \(X_AX_B\ket{111}=\ket{001}\), both orthogonal to the state, so \(\langle X_AX_B\rangle=0\). Alice’s and Bob’s \(X\) outcomes are uncorrelated, giving error \(\frac12\) in \(X\) rounds. (c) Complementarity: Eve’s perfect knowledge of \(Z\) forces Alice’s and Bob’s \(X\) correlation to vanish. Low error in one basis together with low error in the complementary basis is what limits an eavesdropper, which is why BB84 tests both.

16-quantum-cryptography.question: The six-state protocol uses the \(Z\), \(X\), and \(Y\) bases, with eigenstates \(\ket0,\ket1\), \(\ket\pm\), and \((\ket0\pm i\ket1)/\sqrt2\), chosen with equal probability by Alice and Bob. (a) What fraction of rounds is sifted? (b) In an intercept-resend attack where Eve picks one of the three bases at random, what sifted error rate results? (c) Compare with BB84’s \(\frac14\), and explain the trade-off.
hints: Eve picks the wrong basis with probability \(\frac23\).
A wrong-basis resend gives Bob a fair result in his basis.
16-quantum-cryptography.answer: (a) Bases match with probability \(\frac13\). (b) Eve chooses the right basis with probability \(\frac13\) (no error) and a wrong one with probability \(\frac23\), after which Bob’s result is a fair coin, so the error is \(\frac23\cdot\frac12=\frac13\). (c) The attack causes \(33\%\) error instead of \(25\%\), so it is easier to detect and the protocol tolerates somewhat more noise. The price is a lower sifting rate, \(\frac13\) instead of \(\frac12\), and a third basis to implement. Using more mutually unbiased bases makes eavesdropping more conspicuous at the cost of efficiency.
